Q: What is the difference between 'Map.entry(k, v)' and 'AbstractMap.SimpleImmutableEntry::new'? A:

As mentioned by @VGR in a comment, you should look at the Javadoc of Map::entry(K,V) and AbstractMap.SimpleImmutableEntry to see their objective differences.

Since (Year) Extendable Allow null Serializable Value-based
Map::entry(K,V) Java 9 (2017) No No No Yes
SimpleImmutableEntry Java 6 (2006) Yes Yes Yes No

And it should be noted that the former is a static factory method, whereas the latter is a class that you instantiate directly via a constructor.

At a more subjective level, the Map::entry(K,V) method is the better designed API for when you simply want an unmodifiable Map.Entry.

  • It's scoped to the Map interface instead of a relatively arbitrary abstract implementation. That makes it more convenient, which was the primary goal of JEP 269: Convenience Factory Methods for Collections, and arguably more readable.
  • The implementation is not public API. That makes it easier to change the implementation as the language evolves.
  • User code can't extend Map::entry(K,V), unlike the non-final SimpleImmutableEntry class. That means there's a stronger guarantee the implementation does not break the contract.

You should prefer Map::entry(K,V) over SimpleImmutableEntry unless you really need to allow null keys or values, or really need the entry to be serializable.

That all said, the primary purpose of Map::entry(K,V) is for creating an unmodifiable Map from entries. For example:

import static java.util.Map.entry;
import java.util.Map;

class Example {

  static final Map<String, String> MAP = Map.ofEntries(
      entry("key1", "value1"),
      entry("key2", "value2"),
      entry("key3", "value3"),
      entry("key4", "value4"),
      entry("key5", "value5"));
}

And the primary purpose of AbstractMap.Simple[Immutable]Entry is to aid in creating your own Map implementation, particularly one that inherits from AbstractMap.

If you need a tuple outside the context of a Map then consider creating a record specific to your domain. At the least, your domain-specific type will have more appropriate naming than the general "Entry", "key", and "value" names. For example, having:

record Point(int x, int y) {}

Would be better than using Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>.

Q: What's the difference between 'git switch' and 'git checkout' <branch>? A:

The switch command indeed does the same thing as checkout, but only for those usages that switch branches. It cannot restore working tree files — that is done using restore, the other command split off from checkout.

The two commands which checkout has been split into, in summary:

  • switch — Switch to a specified branch
  • restore — Restore file(s) from another branch or source

Detailed explanation

As noted in your quote from the 2.23.0 release notes, the switch and restore commands were introduced to split the checkout command into two separate pieces:

  • "checking out a branch to work on advancing its history"
  • "checking out paths out of the index and/or a tree-ish to work on advancing the current history"

In other words, checkout does two different things, and this release split each of those different things into its own focused command.

This dual purpose of checkout can be seen in its summary description in the documentation:

git-checkout - Switch branches or restore working tree files

The commit that added the switch command explains the rationale for the new commands in its commit message:

"git checkout" doing too many things is a source of confusion for many users (and it even bites old timers sometimes). To remedy that, the command will be split into two new ones: switch and restore. The good old "git checkout" command is still here and will be until all (or most of users) are sick of it.

From this, it's clear that the new commands were introduced to reduce confusion by having two focused commands, rather than one multi-purpose command.

Command comparison

I have not found a full comparison of the checkout, switch, and restore commands anywhere. From reading through the documentation, I think this should be a fairly comprehensive comparison:

previous command new command
git checkout <branch> git switch <branch>
git checkout N/A (use git status)
git checkout -b <new_branch> [<start_point>] git switch -c <new-branch> [<start-point>]
git checkout -B <new_branch> [<start_point>] git switch -C <new-branch> [<start-point>]
git checkout --orphan <new_branch> [<start_point>]
then
git rm -rf .		 git switch --orphan <new-branch>
git checkout --orphan <new_branch> [<start_point>] git switch --orphan <new-branch>
then
git restore -s <start_point> --staged --worktree -- .
git checkout [--detach] <commit> git switch --detach <commit>
git checkout --detach [<branch>] git switch --detach [<branch>]
git checkout [--] <pathspec>… git restore [--] <pathspec>…
git checkout --pathspec-from-file=<file> git restore --pathspec-from-file=<file>
git checkout <tree-ish> [--] <pathspec>… git restore -s <tree> [--] <pathspec>…
git checkout <tree-ish> --pathspec-from-file=<file> git restore -s <tree> --pathspec-from-file=<file>
git checkout -p [<tree-ish>] [--] [<pathspec>…] git restore -p [-s <tree>] [--] [<pathspec>…]

As shown by this comparison, some prior usages can be converted to the new commands by simply replacing the old command name (checkout) with the new one (switch, restore), whereas others require additional adjustment.

Notable changes

Notable changes include:

  • The -b/-B options for creating a new branch before switching are renamed to -c/-C. They also have long option variants (--create/--force-create), unlike before.
  • --detach (or -d) is now always required when switching to a detached head, where it was previously optional for commits but required for branches.
  • The source tree for restoring is now given by the -s (or --source) option, rather than being an inline argument.
  • Switching using --orphan starts with an empty index and working tree, rather than using <start_point> (or the current branch, if no <start_point> specified) as the basis of the index and working tree. It also therefore also no longer has the <start_point> option.
  • Switching using --force (or -f) now fails if there are unmerged entries, rather than ignoring them. --force has also been renamed to --discard-changes, with --force being kept as an alias.

Q: What is ubuntu-slim in GitHub Actions? A:

Among GitHub-hosted runners, ubuntu-slim is a container (as opposed to the standard GitHub Actions runners, which are virtual machines) with a single CPU, intended for lightweight tasks (see https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners#single-cpu-runners).

ubuntu-slim runs on Ubuntu 24.04.

The full specifications are documented here: ubuntu-slim-Readme.md

Q: H2 "runscript" command turns all table names into uppercase A:

Another option is to wrap table/column names in double quotes to preserve casing.

E.g. create table "products" instead of create table products

Q: How to develop software that contains more than 20,000 lines of code? A:

Translation units only exist until the final program is linked. So conceptually you should think of them all as being one monolithic entity - with the proviso that you have no control over which order they are initialised in. So you have to be very careful with global data.

If you need global data, then look into the Singleton Pattern to find out how to do that safely.

Q: midpoint between two POSIXct times A:

You can do as follows:

data$midtime <- as.POSIXct((as.numeric(data$stoptime) + as.numeric(data$starttime)) / 2, origin = '1970-01-01')
